unit.unitOverview: You already know that light travels in straight lines and bounces off surfaces. This unit takes both a step further: it shows exactly where a ray goes when it strikes a mirror, and what happens to it when it passes from air into water or glass. Two rules, both of which you can measure, and between them they explain mirrors, lenses, rainbows and why a straw in a glass looks broken.

objectives.text: Describe how a ray of light changes direction when it is reflected from a plane mirror.
Describe how a ray of light changes direction when it travels through different mediums and know that this is called refraction.

sourceDocuments: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 6, topics on reflection and refraction
provenance.transformation: Authored against Cambridge Primary Science 0097 — Stage 6 from the Cambridge books, for a sub-strand the source pack does not cover.

outcomes: Describe how a ray of light changes direction when it reflects from a plane mirror.
Measure the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection and compare them.
Use the law of reflection to predict where a reflected ray will go.
Describe what happens to a ray of light passing from one medium into another.
Name that change of direction as refraction and explain what causes it.
Explain everyday effects, such as a straw appearing bent, using refraction.

concepts.title: What a Ray Does at a Mirror
concepts.explanation:
A PLANE MIRROR is a flat mirror, and what a light ray does when it strikes one is precise enough to be a law.

First the words, because they have to be exact. The ray arriving is the INCIDENT ray; the ray leaving is the REFLECTED ray. Draw a line at right angles to the mirror at the point where the ray hits, and that line is the NORMAL. The ANGLE OF INCIDENCE is between the incident ray and the normal. The ANGLE OF REFLECTION is between the reflected ray and the normal. Note that both angles are measured from the NORMAL and not from the mirror's surface - measuring from the surface is the commonest error here, and it gives the wrong number every time even though the two angles still come out equal.

The LAW OF REFLECTION is then short: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Shine a ray in at 30 degrees to the normal and it leaves at 30 degrees on the other side. At 50 it leaves at 50. Straight at the mirror - zero degrees - and it comes straight back along its own path.

Because the law is exact, reflection is predictable, and that is what makes mirrors useful rather than merely shiny. You can work out before you start where a ray will go, which is how a periscope is designed, how a dentist's mirror is angled, and how a driver's mirror is set to show the road behind.

Why a mirror and not a wall? Both reflect light. A mirror's surface is so smooth that all the rays arriving together leave together, still in order, so the pattern survives and you see an image. A wall is rough at a small scale, so the rays scatter in every direction - you see the wall, and no image in it.
concepts.example: A ray box shines a beam onto a mirror on a sheet of paper. Mark the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal, then measure both angles with a protractor: 34 and 34. Turn the mirror a little and measure again: 51 and 51. The two are equal every time, to within the degree a protractor can read.

concepts.title: Light Changes Direction Between Materials
concepts.explanation:
Light travels in straight lines - through one material. Send it from one material into another and it changes direction at the boundary, and that change is called REFRACTION.

The material light travels through is called a MEDIUM: air, water and glass are the three that matter here. Light moves fastest in air, more slowly in water, and slower still in glass. That difference in speed is the whole cause of refraction, and it is worth stating plainly, because 'light bends' sounds like magic until you know why.

A useful picture: imagine a line of people walking in step across a field and entering deep mud at an angle. The first person to reach the mud slows down while the others are still on grass, so the whole line pivots. Light does the same thing at the boundary, for the same reason.

The direction of the bend follows a rule. Going from a faster medium into a slower one - air into water or glass - the ray bends TOWARDS the normal. Going the other way, from slower to faster, it bends AWAY from the normal. And a ray arriving exactly along the normal, straight on, does not bend at all, because there is no side to slow down first.

So two different things can happen to a ray at a boundary, and they are worth keeping apart. At a mirror it bounces back and the angles are equal - reflection. At the surface of water or glass it passes through and changes direction - refraction. At a window you get both at once, which is why you can see the street and faintly see yourself.
concepts.example: Shine a narrow beam at an angle into a tank of water. You can see the beam kink sharply at the surface, bending towards the normal as it enters. Aim it straight down instead and it goes through without bending at all - the same water, the same light, and no bend, because nothing entered first.

concepts.title: What Refraction Explains
concepts.explanation:
Refraction is not a laboratory curiosity. Once you can see it, a set of everyday puzzles all turn out to be the same thing.

A STRAW IN A GLASS OF WATER looks bent or broken at the surface. It is perfectly straight. Light from the underwater part of the straw bends as it leaves the water and enters the air, so it reaches your eye from a slightly different direction than it started - and your brain, which assumes light travels in straight lines, places that part of the straw where the light appears to have come from.

A COIN AT THE BOTTOM OF A BUCKET looks nearer the surface than it is, and water is always shallower to look at than to step into. The same bending, and the same assumption by the brain, is why.

A FISH seen from the bank is not quite where it appears, which anyone who has tried to spear one learns quickly.

A LENS is refraction put to work on purpose. A curved piece of glass bends every ray that enters it by a controlled amount, so all the rays from one point can be brought back together at another point. That is the whole principle of a magnifying glass, a camera, a pair of spectacles and the lens inside your own eye.

And a RAINBOW is refraction plus one extra fact: the different colours in white light bend by slightly different amounts. Each raindrop refracts the sunlight entering it, reflects it off the inside of the back of the drop, and refracts it again on the way out - and because the colours bend differently, they leave separated.
concepts.example: Put a coin in an opaque cup and step back until the rim just hides it. Keep still while someone pours water in, and the coin comes into view without anything moving. The light from it is now bending as it leaves the water, arriving at your eye from a direction it could not have taken before.

concepts.title: Two Rules, Side by Side
concepts.explanation:
This unit has two laws, and the useful thing is to be able to say which one applies before you start drawing.

REFLECTION happens when light meets a surface it cannot pass through, and comes back. The rule is that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal. The medium does not change, because the light never enters the mirror.

REFRACTION happens when light passes from one transparent medium INTO another, and continues on a new course. The rule is about direction: into a slower medium it bends towards the normal, into a faster one away from it, and straight along the normal it does not bend at all. The medium does change, which is the entire cause.

So the question to ask is whether the light passed through the boundary or came back off it. Passed through means refraction; came back means reflection.

Most real surfaces do both. A window reflects a little and transmits most, which is why shop glass shows you a faint version of yourself over the display. Water does both too - a lake reflects the sky and you can also see the stones on the bottom, and which one dominates depends on the angle you are looking from. Standing right over it you see the stones; looking across it from low down you see the sky.

And one thing neither rule permits: light does not turn corners on its own. Both laws describe what happens AT a boundary. In between, in a single medium, light travels in straight lines, which is why you cannot see round a wall and why shadows have edges.
concepts.example: Look into a still pool from directly above and you see the bottom, because most of the light is refracting up out of the water to your eye. Crouch down and look across the same pool at a shallow angle and you see the sky and the trees instead - most of the light now reflecting off the surface. Same water, two rules, and the angle decides.

explorations.title: Measuring the Two Angles
explorations.context: To test the law of reflection by measuring, rather than taking it on trust.
explorations.prompt: Stand a mirror upright on paper and shine a narrow beam at it. Mark the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal. Measure both angles with a protractor. Repeat at five different angles.
explorations.answer: The angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are equal at every setting, to within a degree or two - which is the reading error of a protractor, not a real difference.
explorations.hint: Draw the normal FIRST, at right angles to the mirror where the beam hits. Measuring from the mirror's surface instead is the mistake that spoils this experiment.
explorations.explanation: What a Ray Does at a Mirror: the law of reflection says the two angles are equal, both measured from the normal - which is what makes a mirror predictable.

explorations.title: Watching a Beam Bend
explorations.context: To see refraction happen and find out when it does not.
explorations.prompt: Shine a narrow beam into a tank of water at a steep angle, then a shallow one, then straight down. Sketch the path each time and describe when the bend is largest and when there is none.
explorations.answer: The beam bends towards the normal on entering the water, and the bend is largest at the shallowest angle. Aimed straight along the normal there is no bend at all.
explorations.hint: A little milk or chalk dust in the water makes the beam visible all the way through instead of only where it enters.
explorations.explanation: Light Changes Direction Between Materials: refraction happens because light travels at different speeds in different media, and a ray arriving straight on has no side to slow first.

explorations.title: The Coin That Reappears
explorations.context: To use refraction to explain something that looks impossible.
explorations.prompt: Put a coin in an opaque cup and step back until the rim just hides it. Stay completely still while someone slowly pours water in. Describe what happens and explain it with a ray diagram.
explorations.answer: The coin comes into view without anyone moving. Light from it now refracts as it leaves the water, arriving at your eye from a direction it could not have travelled before.
explorations.hint: You must not move at all, or you will have changed the one thing the experiment depends on.
explorations.explanation: What Refraction Explains: your brain assumes light travelled in a straight line, so it places the coin where the light appears to have come from.

methods.title: Drawing a Reflected Ray
methods.example: To predict where a ray will go after it hits a plane mirror.
steps: Draw the mirror as a straight line and mark where the ray strikes it.
Draw the normal: a dashed line at right angles to the mirror at that point.
Measure the angle between the incident ray and the normal.
Draw the reflected ray on the other side of the normal at exactly the same angle.
Label both angles and mark them equal.
Check: both angles measured from the NORMAL, never from the mirror.

methods.title: Drawing a Refracted Ray
methods.example: To show what happens to a ray passing from air into water or glass.
steps: Draw the boundary as a straight line and mark where the ray meets it.
Draw the normal at right angles to the boundary at that point.
Decide which way the ray is going: into a slower medium, or out into a faster one.
Into a slower medium, draw the ray continuing but bent TOWARDS the normal; out into a faster one, bend it AWAY.
If the ray arrives along the normal, draw it straight through with no bend.
Label the media on each side, since the bend depends entirely on which is which.

methods.title: Explaining an Everyday Effect
methods.example: To account for something that looks wrong, using reflection or refraction.
steps: Say whether the light passed through a boundary or bounced off it - that chooses your rule.
Identify the two media, if it passed through.
Sketch the real path of the light from the object to the eye, with the bend at the boundary.
Now sketch the straight line the eye ASSUMES the light came along.
Where those two lines disagree is where the object appears to be, and that is your explanation.

workedExamples.title: A ray at 40 degrees
workedExamples.prompt: A ray strikes a plane mirror at 40 degrees to the normal. At what angle does it leave, and in which direction?
workedExamples.solution: At 40 degrees to the normal, on the opposite side of the normal from the incident ray. The law of reflection says the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, so 40 in means 40 out - and the ray leaves on the other side of the normal, not back along the same side.

workedExamples.title: Why a wall has no reflection in it
workedExamples.prompt: A mirror and a white wall both reflect light. Why can you see your face in only one of them?
workedExamples.solution: A mirror's surface is smooth enough that rays arriving together leave together, keeping their arrangement, so the pattern of light from your face survives and forms an image. A wall is rough at a very small scale, so each ray leaves in its own direction and the pattern is scattered. Both reflect; only one preserves the image.

workedExamples.title: The broken straw
workedExamples.prompt: Explain why a straight straw looks bent where it enters a glass of water.
workedExamples.solution: The straw is straight. Light from the underwater part bends as it leaves the water and enters the air, so it reaches your eye from a different direction than it set off in. Your brain assumes light travels in straight lines and places that part of the straw along the line the light arrived on - which is not where it actually is. The result is a visible kink exactly at the water's surface, where the bending happens.

workedExamples.title: A ray that does not bend
workedExamples.prompt: A ray enters a glass block and continues in a perfectly straight line. What can you conclude?
workedExamples.solution: That it arrived along the normal - straight on to the surface, at zero degrees. Refraction happens because one side of the beam enters the slower medium before the other and slows first, which pivots it. A ray arriving square to the surface has no side entering first, so there is nothing to pivot and it passes straight through, even though it does slow down.

activities.title: The protractor test
activities.materials: A small flat mirror, paper, a pencil, a protractor, and a narrow beam of light or sunlight through a slit in card.
steps: Stand the mirror upright on the paper and draw a line along its base.
Shine the beam at the mirror and mark two points on the incoming beam and two on the outgoing one.
Take the mirror away and join the marks, then draw the normal where the rays meet.
Measure both angles and record them. Repeat at five different angles and write down whether the pairs matched.

activities.title: Bent straws and vanishing coins
activities.materials: A clear glass, a straw or straight stick, an opaque cup, a coin, water.
steps: Stand the straw in the empty glass and look at it from the side. Add water and look again.
Sketch what you see before and after, marking exactly where the kink appears.
Put the coin in the opaque cup and back away until the rim hides it, then have water poured in while you hold still.
Write one explanation that accounts for BOTH observations, using refraction.

activities.title: Which rule is this?
activities.materials: A notebook, and a walk around where you live.
steps: Find six situations involving light: a window, a puddle, a spoon in a cup, a mirror, a shiny pot, a pair of spectacles.
For each, write down whether the light came back off a boundary or passed through it.
Name the rule that applies, and say which observation told you.
Mark any situation where BOTH are happening, and say how you can tell.

rules.text: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection - both measured from the NORMAL.
Light refracts because it travels at different speeds in different media.
Into a slower medium a ray bends towards the normal; into a faster one, away from it.
A ray arriving along the normal does not bend at all.

terms: The ray of light arriving at a surface.
The ray of light leaving a surface after reflection.
A line at right angles to a surface at the point a ray strikes it.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
The change of direction of light passing from one medium into another.
The material light is travelling through - air, water or glass.
A curved piece of glass that refracts rays by a controlled amount.
The picture of an object formed by light, as in a mirror.
commonMistakes: The angles are measured from the mirror's surface.
They are measured from the NORMAL, the line at right angles to the surface. Measuring from the surface gives the wrong number every time, even though the two still come out equal.
It changes direction because it travels at a different speed in the new medium, and one side of the beam enters first. No speed change, no bend.
A straw in water is really bent.
It is perfectly straight. The light from its lower part bends on leaving the water, and the brain places the straw along the line the light arrived on.
Reflection and refraction are the same thing.
Reflection comes back off a boundary; refraction passes through it. A window does both at once, which is why you see the street and faintly yourself.
A rough wall does not reflect light.
It reflects it in all directions at once, which is why you can see the wall. A mirror is simply smooth enough to keep the rays in order, so an image survives.

connections.text: A driver's mirror is angled using the law of reflection: the angle it is set at decides exactly which piece of road comes into view.
A fish is never quite where it looks, because the light from it bends on leaving the water - which is why spearing one takes practice.
Every lens is refraction used on purpose, bending rays by a controlled amount so they meet again at one point.
A rainbow is refraction twice and reflection once inside every raindrop, with the colours separating because each bends by a slightly different amount.

realProblems.context: A shopkeeper wants a mirror high in the corner so that from the till she can see the doorway she cannot otherwise see.
realProblems.prompt: How would you work out the angle to fix it at?
realProblems.answer: Draw the light path from the doorway to the mirror to her eye. At the mirror, the incoming and outgoing rays must make equal angles with the normal, so the mirror has to be turned until its normal bisects the angle between those two directions. Fixing it by guesswork and adjusting is the same thing done slowly.
realProblems.hint: The mirror's normal must sit exactly halfway between the two directions.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Set the mirror so its normal bisects the angle between the line to the doorway and the line to her eye - that is the law of reflection applied.

realProblems.context: A child wading into a river says the water is much deeper than it looked from the bank.
realProblems.prompt: Explain why water always looks shallower than it is.
realProblems.answer: Light from the riverbed bends away from the normal as it leaves the water into the air, so it reaches the eye from a steeper direction than it set off. The brain assumes a straight path and places the bed higher up than it really is, making the water look shallower.
realProblems.hint: The bed appears wherever the arriving light SEEMS to have come from.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Refraction at the surface makes light from the bed arrive from a steeper direction, so the bed appears raised and the water looks shallower.

realProblems.context: Someone claims a shop window 'is a mirror at night and a window in the day', and that the glass must change.
realProblems.prompt: Correct them using both rules from this unit.
realProblems.answer: The glass does not change at all. It always reflects a little and transmits most. In daylight the light coming from the street is far brighter than the light inside, so what you mostly see is the transmitted view. At night the inside is brighter than the street, so the small reflected part is what dominates and you see yourself. Same glass, same two rules, different brightness on the two sides.
realProblems.hint: Ask what changed between day and night - the glass, or the light on each side of it?
realProblems.errorFeedback: The glass reflects a little and transmits most at all times; what changes is which side is brighter.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why must both angles in a reflection be measured from the normal rather than from the mirror?
keyIdeas: The normal is at right angles to the surface
It gives one fixed reference for both angles
Measuring from the surface gives a different number
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The normal is a single fixed line at right angles to the surface, so both angles are measured against the same reference and can be fairly compared. Measuring from the mirror's surface gives the complementary angle instead - 60 where the true angle is 30 - and although the two still come out equal as each other, every number is wrong and any prediction made from them fails. It also stops working entirely for a curved mirror, where 'the surface' has no single direction.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why a ray entering water along the normal does not bend, when one entering at an angle does.
keyIdeas: Refraction is caused by a change of speed
At an angle, one side of the beam enters first
Along the normal, the whole beam enters together
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Refraction happens because light travels more slowly in water, and at an angle one side of the beam reaches the water before the other. That side slows first while the rest is still in air, so the beam pivots - like a line of people walking into mud at an angle. A ray arriving straight along the normal has its whole width entering at the same instant, so nothing slows before anything else and there is nothing to pivot. The light still slows down; it simply carries straight on.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain what the bent-straw illusion tells us about how seeing works.
keyIdeas: The brain assumes light travelled in a straight line
The light actually bent at the surface
We see objects where the light SEEMS to come from
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The straw is straight and the illusion is in the seeing, not the straw. Light from the underwater part bends as it leaves the water, so it arrives at the eye along a different line than it set out on. The brain has no way of knowing that and works on the assumption light travels in straight lines, so it traces the arriving ray straight back and places that part of the straw along it. What this shows is that we do not see objects directly - we see where the light appears to have come from, and any bend on the way puts the object somewhere it is not.

questions.question: You can see your face in a mirror but not in a white wall because:

the wall absorbs all the light
the wall does not reflect light
the mirror makes its own light

the straw really bends in water

glass only reflects in the dark
